AM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
w Determine if an AM transmitter and receiver system is operating correctly.
w Identify the faulted circuit in a malfunctioning AM transmitter and receiver system.

In this lesson you will troubleshoot faults in an AM transmitter and receiver system.
INTRODUCTIONM
Troubleshooting AM systems is a bit more complex but not any more difficult than troubleshooting individual circuits.
First you isolate the fault to a particular section........

After the fault has been isolated to the section (transmitter or receiver) the faulty circuit should be identified. Then you can make resistance, voltage and current measurements to find the bad component.

AM CIRCUIT TROUBLESHOOTING
In this experiment you will locate the failed circuit in an AM transmitter and receiver system.
EXPERIMENT
The transmitter is located on the PC130-91 card............
It contains an oscillator circuit and a modulator circuit.m
The receiver is located on the PC130-92 card...............
It contains a RF amplifier circuit, demodulator circuit and two AF amplifier circuits.
To locate a faulted circuit you must first determine if the AM system is operating correctly.
This is done by using the oscilloscope to measure the receiver output.
If you have a good signal on PC130-92 Pin T, the transmitter and receiver must be operating correctly.
If you do not have a good signal on PC130-92 Pin T the AM system is faulted.
Once you have determined that the AM system is not operating correctly you must then isolate the fault to either the transmitter, transmission medium or receiver.
This is accomplished by making two simple oscilloscope measurements.
First, measure the output of the transmitter.
If an AM signal is present on TP3 the transmitter circuit must be operating correctly.
If the AM signal is not present the transmitter is faulted.
Second, measure the receiver input. The receiver output was checked in the beginning to determine whether the system was operating, so this does not need to be rechecked.
If an attenuated AM signal is not present on Pin E, the fault is in the transmission medium.
If an attenuated AM signal is present on Pin E, the fault is in the receiver.
If the fault is in the transmission medium, checking out the antenna or transmission cables will normally locate the failure.
If the fault is in the transmitter, oscilloscope measurements on TP1, TP2 and TP3 will isolate the fault to the oscillator or modulator circuit.
If the fault is in the receiver, oscilloscope measurements on TP1, TP2, TP3 and TP4 will isolate the fault to the RF amp, demodulator or AF amp circuits.

Voltage and resistance measurements can be made to determine the bad component after the failed circuit is identified. In this lesson you are not required to troubleshoot down to the component level because we use basic amplifiers, oscillators, modulator and demodulator circuits.
